extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and respondents in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) proceedings; patent/trademark attorneys and agents
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules the USPTO (OED) and Administrative Law Judge apply when assessing practitioner misconduct, default judgment, and sanctions in disciplinary proceedings before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service by mail / completion of service
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint or other papers may be mailed to a respondent at their address of record provided the delivery service allows for confirmation of delivery. 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2), § 11.42(b)(2). Service by mail is completed when the document is mailed. 37 C.F.R. § 11.42(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a delivery service that permits confirmation of delivery (e.g., certified mail). Service is deemed complete upon mailing (not receipt); evidence of mailing and signed-for delivery to the address of record supports proper service (as shown by certified-mail delivery signed at respondent's address).

rubrics_metrics.name: Default for failure to timely file an answer
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in default judgment." 37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent does not timely answer a Complaint, the allegations may be deemed admitted and a Motion for Default Judgment may be granted. An Order to Show Cause may be issued; failure to respond to that Order supports granting default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall "act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client." 37 C.F.R. § 11.103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to prepare, file, or prosecute a client's application, not responding to client communications or status inquiries, and otherwise neglecting a matter violate this duty. Such violations are grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect client's interests; refund unearned advance fees
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall "take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client's interests, such as giving reasonable notice to the client, allowing time for employment of other counsel, surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled and refunding any advance payment of fee or expense that has not been earned or incurred." 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must give reasonable notice before withdrawal, allow time for replacement counsel, return client papers, and refund unearned advance fees. Refusing to refund unearned fees (e.g., retaining an $8,000 advance when no services were performed) violates § 11.116(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation. 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include falsely representing status (signing filings as an attorney when suspended) and refusing to return unearned funds. Such conduct is independently sanctionable under § 11.804(c) (and related provisions such as 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on practicing law in violation of jurisdictional regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall 'not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction.'" 37 C.F.R. § 11.505.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To handle certain matters (e.g., trademark matters), a practitioner must be a member in good standing of the highest court of a State. Continuing to represent clients before the USPTO while suspended from state bars violates § 11.505.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to cooperate with OED / respond to lawful demands
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall not 'fail to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline in an investigation of any matter before it, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority.'" 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to Requests for Information (RFIs) or OED letters is a violation. Non-cooperation can both constitute a separate violation and be treated as aggravating in sanction analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall not 'engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.'" 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusal to cooperate with investigations and other obstructive behaviors can be found prejudicial to the administration of justice and support disciplinary sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conduct reflecting adversely on practitioner's fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall not 'engage in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.'" 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision covers additional conduct not explicitly listed elsewhere; absence of other allegations may mean § 11.804(i) is not violated in a given case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate citation prohibiting dishonesty/fraud (professional rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) also states that a practitioner shall not 'engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, and misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple ethics/regulatory provisions may overlap in prohibiting dishonest conduct; the existence of parallel rules (e.g., §10.23(b)(4)) reinforces the applicability of sanctions for dishonest acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider before imposing sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors. 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four factors form the central framework for determining the severity of discipline (ranging from reprimand to exclusion). Each factor is assessed on the record: (1) identify duties violated; (2) assess mental state—intentional/knowing supports harsher sanction; (3) quantify actual and potential injury to client/public/system; (4) identify aggravating (dishonest motive, pattern, obstruction, lack of remorse) and mitigating factors. The Court applied all four and found they supported exclusion in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards and identification of aggravating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court routinely looks to the American Bar Association Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions when assessing attorney disciplinary sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors the Court may consider (and which the record here showed) include dishonest/selfish motive (e.g., retaining unearned advance), failure to acknowledge misconduct or make restitution, a pattern of misconduct (repeated failures to respond), and obstruction of the disciplinary process. Presence of aggravating factors and absence of mitigation favors more severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on respondent to raise mitigating circumstances / affirmative defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden is on Respondent to raise any affirmative defenses or mitigating circumstances and specify their nexus to the misconduct and any reason they may provide a defense or mitigation. 37 C.F.R. § 11.36(c) and § 11.49.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent fails to appear and defend, they forfeit the opportunity to present mitigating evidence; absence of mitigation supports imposition of maximum sanction consistent with other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of practitioner status upon suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may change a practitioner's USPTO status (e.g., from 'attorney' to 'agent') when the practitioner is suspended from the practice of law in a state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a change is informational and may be used to notify practitioners and the public of a restriction; continuing to sign filings as an 'Attorney of Record' while suspended is a separate violation under the rules prohibiting misrepresentation and unauthorized practice.
